The second question that arises is: If we do not have any standards or criteria, what is the minister or his department going to use in deciding whether or not the water quality management plans that he proposes are satisfactory? I tried to get an answer to this question from various people in the department, including Dr. Tinney who was the main witness from the department. I asked him, "What kind of standard are you going to use in the department?" I asked the question because under this bill, when a water quality management area is set up the board or commission has to decide on what sort of standards it wants for its area, for its waters. It has to decide how to achieve those standards, at what cost, and so forth.
Having made up such a plan, the board then presents it to the minister for approval. The fundamental part of such a plan is the standard to which waters are to be elevated or at which they are to be maintained. This is what a water board is supposed to decide, and then it is written specifically in this legislation that the minister must consider that proposal and decide whether or not it is satisfactory. What basis is the minister or his department going to use? Nothing in this respect is set out in the bill, and there can be nothing in the regulations because there is no provision in the bill for making regulations. This is what we have been trying to do. We have not even been trying to write the regulations. We have been trying to put a clause in the bill so that the minister can write the regulations. It occurred to me as I listened to the remarks made only by hon. members on this side of the House, and as I read some of the Minutes of the committee discussion, that if someone from another planet were to come here and listen to our debate, he would wonder what it was all about. I agree with the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) that there really ought to be an explanation as to why the minister finds so unacceptable the simple suggestions made in the two motions we are debating. I see he is busy on work which I am sure is important. All that these proposed amendments say is that the act ought to give the Governor in Council authority to set national quality standards for various classes of water. The proposed amendments do not even attempt to set the standards that the Governor in Council ought to introduce. That idea was contained in another motion which was not found acceptable. The motions we are now debating merely say that the act ought to give the government power to proclaim national quality standards for various classes of water. Why that should be unacceptable to the minister and to the government, I simply do not understand.
It has occurred to me in the last few months that people will consider the fight against pollution to be in the same category as motherhood. It is something that everyone ought to be concerned about. We satisfy ourselves with declaring we are sorry to see the pollution which threatens our people. We say in ringing terms that it is necessary for us to be rid of it and yet, sadly, we do relatively little about it.
This act, part of which we are now discussing, is an example of the very small step we are taking on a matter that everybody proclaims to be of the utmost urgency for the future welfare of all mankind. Professor Richard A. Falk of Princeton and of the Centre for Advanced Study in the Behavioural Sciences says:
The planet and mankind are in grave danger of irreversible catastrophe ... Man may be skeptical about following the flight of the dodo into extinction, but the evidence points increasingly to just such a pursuit... There are four interconnected threats to the planet-wars of mass destruction, overpopulation, pollution, and the depletion of resources. They have a cumulative effect. A problem in one area renders it more difficult to solve the problems in any other area.
I draw the attention of hon. members particularly to the last sentence of the quotation:
The basis of all four problems is the inadequacy of the sovereign states to manage the affairs of mankind in the twentieth century.
May 21, 1970

Water Resources Programs
This is precisely the case in this country as in all other countries that have the questionable benefit of being highly industrialized and which are faced with threats to the welfare of mankind which industrialization, necessary though it is, has produced for ordinary people in all parts of the world. It is our failure as a sovereign state to deal with pollution and the other matters mentioned by Professor Falk that worries the people of Canada and worries, I am sure, the minister. I assume that the minister and his colleagues are just as worried about pollution and the threat it holds for human welfare in Canada as are the people of Canada and the members on this side of the House.
When we move these amendments, it is not for the purpose of putting the minister on the spot. It is for the purpose of pleading with him to strengthen the act which in our view does no more than set up the necessary machinery. It does not provide the other things which are also necessary to make that machinery do the job which has to be performed.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
When I consider, as a layman, this dreadful problem of pollution, when I see what has happened to many of our rivers and lakes, when I see, as I go about this country, industries which are constantly polluting the waters and the air around them, I ask myself: What is it that we need in order to deal with this danger with some effectiveness, realizing that it will be a matter of decades or even generations before the water and the air can be cleaned? It seems to me that the following things at least are necessary. First, it is necessary to have an objective. It is necessary to set national standards for the various classes of water so that the community as a whole may have a goal toward which it is working and for whose achievement it is spending whatever money may be available for the purpose. Second, there must be massive funds available for the job, funds which will finance the building of the capital equipment required if we are to avoid what is happening now to our waters across Canada.
The cleansing of our waters will not take place in the absence of research funds. Massive amounts are required to enable the municipalities which are now abusing their waters by letting the refuse and pollutants from the ordinary life of the community run into waters such as the St. Lawrence River at Montreal and other rivers across this country,

to construct the capital works required to eliminate such practices. Third, what is obviously necessary in a country such as Canada is the machinery to co-ordinate federal, provincial and municipal efforts in this field. I emphasize the word "municipal" because I do not think the cleansing of our waters is possible unless the municipalities or regional governments take an active part in the process and are allotted the necessary financial resources to build the structure required to avoid the further pollution of the waters they are now polluting.
Fourth, it seems to me there should be national standards, to which strict prohibitory measures are attached to prevent industry, municipalities or individuals from polluting our waters. No anti-pollution measure is worth the paper it is written on, it seems to me, unless it deals with these four major areas. The Canada Water Act does not do so, Mr. Speaker. There is, it is true, one exception. The bill deals with the area of co-ordination of federal and provincial action-not with federal-provincial-municipal action-and provides machinery for co-operation and coordination. To this extent it is a worth while piece of legislation. But it fails to deal with any of the other factors, and in these circumstances it is of little value; it is certainly of much less value than legislation in 1970 on this subject ought to be.
So we start with our first point. It was not possible for members of this House who are not members of the government to move anything which would have the effect of amending the act with respect to funds available to regions and municipalities. Your Honour will recall that you were obliged to rule out one amendment which dealt with federal grants and that several other proposed amendments which involved expenditure were similarly ruled out of order. We know that such amendments cannot be debated on the floor because of the entirely proper and acceptable rules of this Parliament. Nevertheless, we cannot deal with the major problem of financing the anti-pollution work which has to take place, without financing it isn't going to be done. I almost said "it ain't going to be done" as being more appropriate to the subject of pollution we are discussing. We have attempted to stress the criminal aspect of pollution but the minister has refused to adopt our suggestions. So our members have been able only to seek to persuade the government to accept the notion that this bill ought to
May 21, 1970	COMMONS
contain a provision enabling the government to set national standards governing the various classes of water in Canada.
It may be difficult to do so. Perhaps one of the reasons the minister does not want this power is that he sees all kinds of difficulties attached to it. I am sure it would not be easy to set out all the standards which might subsequently be required. This is one of the reasons we believe it should be exercised by way of regulation approved by the Governor in Council. The minister could take some time in producing these standards. One of them, which it is obviously necessary to establish immediately, as soon as the act comes into force, would ensure that none of the waters across Canada shall be permitted to deteriorate below their present level. This would be a start. Even if the government established a regulation which said nothing more than that, we would have taken a step to prevent waters which are not now polluted from being polluted, and to prevent those waters which are only slightly polluted from being further polluted. What is wrong with that? What possible objection could there be to the government taking the power to set national standards so that we might have a starting point for any of the work which is to follow?
There are one or two other simple standards which even laymen can think of. The value of getting them into the act in such a way as to give the government authority to make regulations on the subject is that the minister will be in a position to produce regulations embodying certain standards within a few days of the legislation coming into force. He could then study the situation further and produce revised standards six months later and further standards, if required, in a year or in two years' time. So if he were out about this matter the minister would accept an amendment of this kind giving himself the power progressively to produce standards as he learns more from experience and from studies of various bodies of water in Canada, beginning with the basic ones I have mentioned and building up a set of standards in the course of two or three years which would stand the test of time.
There is another reason which so far has not been mentioned in favour of national standards along the lines suggested by other speakers and by myself. I am thinking of the educational value. I started by saying I was afraid that the subject of anti-pollution is rather like motherhood-everyone is for it. I
DEBATES	7199
Water Resources Programs think this is true of the people of Canada as well as all of us in Parliament. Almost every Canadian says, "It is a pity that the waters are polluted. Something should be done about it". Yet very few Canadians are yet ready to realize that certain payments will be required in order to rid ourselves of polluted waters; that we will have to exercise certain disciplines in personal matters, whether in our homes, in our cottages or in the kind of detergents we use for washing our clothes.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Anti-pollution measures, properly applied, sincerely applied, effectively applied, will require sacrifice on the part of the Canadian people. Anti-pollution will require self-discipline in the way we behave in our homes and in our lives. It will require an understanding of what is involved. One requirement of antipollution measures is education of the people of Canada to what is really meant. We must persuade them that we are not using mere words or being holy about the subject; that we are not just saying that we are against sin. We must persuade them that we mean to tackle the problem of pollution of our waters and of our air and that we really intend to do something about it. One advantage of setting national standards is that this would be spelled out to the people of Canada. It would tell the people of Canada that this is the objective that Parliament and the government have in mind. The minister would say to the people of Canada, "This is the objective I have in mind as the minister responsible. I am not just saying that pollution is a bad thing; I have the authority of Parliament to set standards of quality for Canada's water, standards that I intend will be observed".
I am not going to say what these standards should be. I am trying to avoid repeating things that have already been said. However, what I do not understand is why the minister is refusing to accept these simple motions. I could be suspicious enough to wonder whether the minister really intends this act to do something about pollution, or whether it is merely a piece of window-dressing that he will be able to wave in the air at the appropriate time for the appropriate purpose. I have a feeling-I say this sincerely-that that would be totally unfair to the minister. I have a feeling that he is genuine in his desire to do something about the pollution of Canadian waters. On that assumption, his obstinacy in regard to these simple amendments is inexplicable. We are not-

Mr. Speaker, I have reached what might be called a peroration so I will not have to worry members for very long. The minister's obstinacy in this matter is inexplicable. These motions are not asking him at this moment to write the standards, but merely give him authority under the act to do so. He does not have to produce all the standards at one time. He can produce them one by one, two by two or three by three over a period of months, or even two or three years, as his experience grows and as studies indicate the standards required.
He can do more than that, Mr. Speaker. He can amend the standards. This is the value of a regulation as opposed to a statutory definition. Regulations can be amended without having to come back to Parliament. If a standard that he has proclaimed proves unworkable or inadequate, then by Order in Council he can amend it. All we are asking him to do in these amendments is to agree to take unto himself this power, in order to make the act more meaningful and in order to set an example to the people of Canada. This would make everyone feel that he and the government really mean business in tackling pollution. As I say, I cannot understand why he refuses to accept them. I hope he may yet be persuaded to see, not the light because this bill does not deal with the whole question of pollution, but at least a glimmer of common sense.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when my colleague the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) a few minutes ago referred to the questionable benefits of industrialization, I found myself thinking about the Indians. The connection may not be immediately obvious to the members of this House, but I was thinking in particular of those Indians who dwell and have for a long time dwelt in that part of the country that I represent in this House. If I understand correctly, it is estimated that something like 30 to 40 per cent of the total Indian population of Canada before the arrival of Europeans dwelt in a rather narrow strip of coastal territory adjacent to the broad waters of the Pacific. There they enjoyed

what in many respects was the highest standard of living of any of the inhabitants of North America at that time. This was largely because they had at their doorstep waters that were of a nature and quality to enable the production of food from rich and bountiful resources.
In many ways they reached a level of civilization through their opportunities for leisure and relatively easy ways of providing the necessities of life which indeed is envied by many of us today, and this with all the background of European so-called civilization that our forefathers brought to this country and which we directly or indirectly have been able to enjoy. Their way of life was such that it really in no way affected or altered to any tangible extent the quality of those waters. As long as they alone inhabited that particular area, the richness of their life continued in almost unbelievable abundance.
When I went to live in that area as a small boy, that abundance still existed almost in its original state. It is true that there was the beginning of an industrialized society. However, at that time the total population of the province of British Columbia reached scarcely half a million people. The kinds of industry existing were so scattered and relatively small that while here and there there was a spotty interference with the original quality of those waters, by and large their ability to teem with abundant life had scarcely been touched.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Since the time when I was able to enjoy those surroundings as a boy, the process of industrialization has increased in geometric progression to the point where we now see looming immediately before us a different kind of situation so far as our waters are concerned. Indeed, the pace of that industrialization and the change in the total magnitude of it, both in respect of individual plants and in the collective sense of the total industrial effort, has rapidly moved even in the period since the end of World War II to the point where it is so different in degree that it has become different in kind. There is, therefore, an increasing concern about the results which are becoming so widely apparent in respect of the effect of this industrialization not only on the waters of the lakes and rivers of British Columbia but on the waters of the seas and inlets and indeed of the ocean itself.
As many members of this House well know, many thoughtful scientists are beginning to
May 21, 1970	COMMONS
raise the question of the ultimate capacity of a body of water as huge as the Pacific Ocean to continue to absorb at the current rate the wastes that are being poured into it. They are raising the question that out of the Pacific Ocean, and to a lesser degree the other oceans of the world, the very life-giving oxygen we breathe is being taken. If this process continues, sooner or later we will all choke to death for lack of air if we have not all died because of the various toxic effects to the water and therefore to our food before that process reaches its ultimate point.
It is with knowledge of this type in my mind that I should like to join in this debate for a few minutes. I may not be able to reach the eloquence of my colleagues from Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) and York South, but I too should like to express my concern about the rather lackadaisical attitude of the minister and the government to which he belongs in respect of the approach being suggested by these amendments which are under consideration. I have not had the opportunity to take part in the sessions of the committee which studied this bill, but during this period of time I did find myself involved with other committees studying matters rather closely related to the content of this bill and its announced purpose in respect of dealing with pollution in Canada.
We had the northern inland waters bill and the Arctic water pollution bill before the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development and we had a bill, not quite so directly related, before the External Affairs Committee in respect of our territorial seas and fishing zones. Then in the Committee on Fisheries we considered some rather substantial amendments to the Fisheries Act. I am sure all members of the House, whether or not they have sat on the Fisheries Committee, realize that the questions of water quality and the welfare of our fisheries are very closely related. So the type of considerations involved in the amendments which are proposed at this stage have been very much in my mind in recent weeks as well as in the minds of the members of the New Democratic Party who have taken part in the deliberations of the committee which considered this bill.
As I listened tonight to the discussion in respect of this amendment, particularly by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and the hon. member for York South, my mind went back to the conference on pollution and our environment which was held in
DEBATES	7201
Water Resources Programs Montreal in 1966, which I attended and indeed to which I have referred a number of times in various remarks I have made in this House on different items which have been before us. I should like to emphasize at this point that the ideas and arguments put forward tonight by my colleagues are precisely the basic ideas which emerged from that pollution conference in 1966. Apart from any argumentation and considerations that have been put forward in the Committee hearings on this bill, and the references made to the committee hearings by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, I submit that there does exist a solid body of evidence and thought that was the product of that conference on pollution in 1966.
As I recall, I believe the whole question of what evolved from that conference may be summarized in two ways. One was a consideration of the idea of watershed management. The other was the whole question which has particular reference to the place of the federal Parliament and the federal government in the scheme of things in respect of the idea of setting forth water quality standards that would be applicable anywhere in Canada and which could be applied in the appropriate way anywhere in Canada. This bill purports to touch on both these areas, though inadequately in my opinion. So far as water quality management on a water basin basis is concerned, in my view the bill is very fuzzy and incomplete. It does not make this concept clear in its reference to water quality management agencies. This idea cannot conceivably develop from that section of the bill.
However, no real assurance has been given, so far as I am aware-and I think there has been some assurance to the contrary-that that idea of watershed management will emerge from this bill. But in the other area, the basic thing that emerges from that conference is completely lacking because if this amendment should be refused the bill would make no provision for the development of adequate water quality standards. I again emphasize, as one or two of my colleagues have, that we are talking about standards in the plural and not in the rather strange way the minister did in trying to suggest we want every water in Canada to be as pure as Lake Louise. I do not know whether I told the minister this, but when I visited the park as a member of the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development I found that the water of Lake Louise was not too pristine pure because waste was being dumped into
May 21, 1970

Water Resources Programs that lake in one of our national parks. If the minister wishes verification of this statement, all he need do is go swimming there.
I think I should again emphasize the nature of the conference to which I referred, particularly because in respect of this bill I notice from various press reports that some constitutional questions have been raised by such eminent figures as the Premier of the province of Ontario.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
Therefore, I think it is not inappropriate to point out that in that conference there were ministers of provincial governments, deputy ministers of provincial governments, pollution control directors and administrators of various provincial governments, a wide range of representatives at the municipal level of government, both elected and appointed, as well as a strong admixture of representatives of various forms of industry and of organizations such as wildlife federations, and so on. Also, a representative of the consumers associations of Canada took an active part in the proceedings. All the questions that arise in this area because we are a federal state, with various responsibilities assigned to various levels of government, emerged in the cross-current of discussion among the various groups at that conference and were battered back and forth.
The pros and cons of both the constitutional and the practical aspects of pollution control were analysed and considered. If there was one clear fact with which everyone seemed to agree no matter what area they came from-I have not in my review of the people who were there mentioned that there were many representatives at the federal level-it was that the federal government should give leadership in the field of water quality maintenance and should take the initiative of setting standards which could be applied right across the country. This is the main purpose and function of a federal government in a federal state, as I see it, otherwise we might as well forget about this place and this government and let each of the ten provinces run its own affairs and do as it pleases in any area of the country.
This is one thing, if nothing more, that I hoped would have emerged in the wake of that conference, that is, a proposal by the government to set standards to which other bodies across the country could reach up, standards which, as the hon. member for York South said, would be moving standards.

By "moving standards" I mean that they would be set by regulation from time to time and would be adjusted with changing technology and more intensive research. After all the time that has elapsed since that conference, with all the heralding that went on year after year by various ministers of the government that we were going to have a Canada Water Act, we find out that standards are the one thing that are lacking in it. So I think it is not unbecoming that a number of us in this House should take the time and effort to stress the need for action and express our regret that the government introducing this piece of legislation has seen fit completely to ignore this fundamental idea.
One of the indirect results of this basic lack in the Canada water bill has been an effort on the part of those of us who for a number of years have been involved in this question through our interest and concern for the welfare of fishermen, to ensure that within that act clear federal jurisdiction is maintained to set standards that will be applicable to all the waters of Canada. It is rather unfortunate in some ways that this has had to happen. In effect, we have had to go behind this act-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the minister has asked me in his absence to reply tonight to the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) who has described himself, I think fairly and aptly, as a mild fellow, and I might say one who is fairly concerned, as are all Canadians, about the proposals for tax reform. This is the sort of discussion that can surely only further the objective of all of us, to have a fair system of tax reform.
The hon. member for Etobicoke (Mr. Gillespie), who made a speech to the Petroleum Accountants Association in Jasper last Thursday, made it abundantly clear in his remarks that he was speaking personally, and this of course is the right and indeed the duty of all Members of Parliament. In commenting on the speech made by the hon. member for Etobicoke I think the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants probably had reference to the Globe and Mail report. That report set out accurately the five special areas that the hon. member dealt with in his remarks. These remarks, Mr. Speaker, are the sort of expression of opinion that the government wants from everyone in Canada. It has been repeated many times that the reason the government put forward its proposals in the form of a white paper is in order that the public will have an opportunity to express its views.
The hon. member for Etobicoke raised the question of whether gains on shares in widely-held companies should be subject to taxation on a different basis than a gain on the sale of shares in other companies, or gains from the sale of other assets, and the distinction between public and private companies with respect to a credit to be given to shareholders in respect of income tax paid by the corporation. This is a very important part of the proposals affecting the taxation of gains and companies, and views about whether it will work or will not work are exactly what the government has requested. The hon. member also made a suggestion for assistance to small corporations. This is an area where a great deal has been said in opposition to the proposal to withdraw the low rate of tax on the first $35,000 of corporation taxable income, but very little has been put forward by way of an alternative.

The government has urged those concerned to make suggestions for ways in which the special problems of small business could be recognized, but not too much has been forthcoming. The government hopes that more Members of Parliament and members of the public will follow the example of the hon. member for Etobicoke and make constructive suggestions in this area.

Mr. Speaker, the "late show" is probably not a very encouraging spot to speak on an issue as vital as the need for updated abortion legislation. Yesterday I tried to get an emergency debate on the matter and it was ruled out of order. Then I asked the Minister of Justice (Mi'. Turner) whether the government contemplated emergency legislation and he told me that no immediate changes were in view.
I call attention to the fact that the public and the press across the country continue to regard the situation of abortions, illegal and otherwise, as a dangerous and growing menace. Newspapers like the Montreal Star, the Windsor Star, the Toronto Globe and Mail and the Vancouver Sun-those four at least, to my certain knowledge-have written editorials pointing out that the present abortion legislation is completely inadequate and needs updating. Evidence about this is coming in from all sides. Here in Ottawa the Association for the Modernization of Abortion Laws has informed me that sometimes it gets as many as ten calls a day from women wanting to know how they can get an illegal abortion or, more properly, illegal in Canada but legal in Britain, Scandinavia and now in New York.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I myself have had a number of telephone calls from women employed in the public service who, finding themselves pregnant, in poor health or in difficult family circumstances and not knowing where to turn, are desperate. The Toronto Globe and Mail carried a very impressive editorial on Tuesday. It quoted a prominent obstetrician as saying that he would hazard a guess that there are at least, nationwide, as many abortions as there are births. When one reflects that in Canada last year there were 370,000 births, one can see that this problem has important and grave dimensions.
May 21, 1970	COMMONS
It is a difficult problem to solve. We know that the legislation is inadequate. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics reports that in the first three months of this year, the three westernmost provinces and the three Maritime provinces reported only 235 therapeutic abortions. When you compare those figures with the evidence of the Toronto obstetrician and of detective Douglas H. Walton of the metro Toronto police morality bureau, that it is quite possible that there are hundreds of illegal abortions in Toronto every week, you begin to realize the pitiful inadequacy of the legislation.
I think the minister should desist from his ostrich-like posture of keeping his head in the sand and thinking that the abortion problem will go away if he stays there long enough. It will not go away. It will increase in size, just like pregnancy. And the pregnant women of Canada in their hundreds and thousands who want and need abortions will not be able to wait. I suggest that we need to do two things. The whole matter ought to be taken out of the Criminal Code and left up to the decision of the woman and her doctor. Even before that legislation becomes possible, we ought to make abortions available not only in hospitals but on an outpatient basis in properly equipped medical clinics and doctors' offices. By using the new suction method machine which is in use in the Ottawa Civic Hospital and in other hospitals across the country, I do not see why this should not be done safely.
Dr. Henry Morgentaler, a respected physician in Montreal, has written to the minister on behalf of the Humanist Association of Canada urging that the medical profession and the Humanist Association be consulted as to how best these changes can be brought about. I urge that this problem be considered as the serious one it is and that there be no further attempts to evade it, because the proportions of the problem will become much greater than they are even at present.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion both in and out of Parliament during discussion of the omnibus criminal law amendment bill last year than did any other matter contained in the legislation. During parliamentary discussion on the omnibus bill the Minister of Justice, as reported on page 4722 of Hansard for January 23, 1969, said:
I realize full well that this matter goes right to the essence of life, goes right to the bone. There is not going to be any consensus on this issue in this house or in the country. There are those on the one hand who abhor abortion for any cause, or for any reason whatsoever. There are those on the other hand who would make abortion wholly permissive or at the personal option of the woman. We have not reached a consensus between those views in this bill. We have reached only what I might call an accommodation. When the life or health of a mother is in jeopardy, therapeutic miscarriage will be absolved from the penalties in the criminal law.
Since enactment of the abortion legislation last year many exaggerated and uninformed statistics have been advanced by proponents of "abortion on demand". For example, it was claimed recently that about 2,000 women a year die from the after effects of abortion. In her remarks this evening the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) quoted some rather fanciful figures that in my submission have no foundation in fact.
I think, it would be better to look at the DBS figures. If we do so, it is difficult to understand the basis on which this claim is made, because the latest statistics available to DBS show that though 22 women died from causes due to abortion in 1964, this number decreased to 13 in 1968. While it is acknowledged that these statistics are incomplete in that they do not represent all provinces, there is nevertheless a wide gap between the two sets of figures.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I can only repeat what the Minister of Justice said in the House yesterday:
We are closely studying the medical experience under the recent amendments to the Criminal Code. When we gather enough information from those statistics we may be in a position to report to the House. At the moment there are no imminent plans to amend the law.
